question: What is your main nursing goal when caring for a patient who just suffered an animal bite or insect sting?

options.A: Discharge the patient with mild analgesics
options.C: Perform surgical debridement of the wound
options.D: Halt toxin exposure and stabilize vital signs

explanation: Great job thinking emergency care! Before cleaning any wound, your priority is making sure the venom stops spreading and the patient's breathing and pulse are steady. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to ask about the type of creature and time of the incident during an assessment?

options.A: It helps determine the correct treatment and predicts potential complications
options.B: It eliminates the need to monitor vital signs over time
options.C: It prevents the patient from panicking about the injury
options.D: It satisfies hospital billing and administrative record requirements

explanation: Knowing what bit or stung the patient (and when!) helps you anticipate symptoms, choose the right antivenom if needed, and watch for trouble early. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h1)

question: Which type of venom component mainly attacks and disrupts nerve signals?
explanation: Think 'neuro' for nerves! Neurotoxins attack the nervous system, which can lead to scary signs like muscle weakness or trouble breathing. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h2)

question: A snakebite patient starts bleeding spontaneously and has abnormal clotting lab results. Which toxin is likely at work?
explanation: Think 'hemo' for blood! Hemotoxins mess with the body's clotting system, causing bleeding and messy lab results. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h2)

question: What is the very first thing you check when a patient arrives with an acute sting?

options.A: Applying a cold ice pack to reduce swelling
options.D: Cleaning the wound with soap and water

explanation: Always ABCs first! Checking airway, breathing, and circulation helps you catch severe allergic reactions or shock before they get out of hand. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h3)

question: A patient arrives with a severe insect sting on their hand, and the hand is swelling up massively. What quick check should you do next?

options.A: Draw blood samples for comprehensive metabolic panels
options.B: Check distal pulses, movement, and sensation in the fingers
options.C: Measure the patient's exact height and weight
options.D: Prepare the patient for immediate surgical amputation

explanation: When a tight space like the hand swells up, blood flow and nerves can get squeezed. Checking fingers for pulses, feeling, and movement helps catch bad circulation early! [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h3)

question: What is the proper way to remove a honeybee stinger stuck in the skin?

options.A: Scrape it gently across the skin using a flat, rigid edge
options.B: Burn the stinger with a heated match to neutralize the venom
options.C: Squeeze the venom sac tightly with metal tweezers and pull straight out
options.D: Scrub the area vigorously with a stiff surgical brush

explanation: Never squeeze a bee stinger! Squeezing pushes more venom into the skin. Instead, gently scrape it away with something flat like a card. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h4)

question: Why do we apply a cold pack to an insect sting right after it happens?

options.A: It numbs the skin permanently to prevent any future scarring
options.B: It constricts blood vessels to slow venom absorption and reduce swelling
options.C: It opens up local capillaries to flush out the venom faster
options.D: It completely neutralizes the chemical composition of the insect toxin

explanation: Cold makes the local blood vessels narrow down (vasoconstriction), slowing down how fast the venom spreads while keeping pain and swelling low. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h4)

question: Which of these actions is a big NO-DO (contraindicated) for a venomous snakebite?

options.A: Positioning the limb at or below heart level
options.B: Transporting the patient to a medical facility promptly
options.C: Applying a tight tourniquet to the bitten limb
options.D: Keeping the patient calm and resting quietly

explanation: Never use a tight tourniquet! It cuts off blood flow completely, causing tissue death. Keep the limb calm and get the patient to the hospital safely. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h5)

question: Why is washing a mammalian bite wound with high-pressure water so important?

options.A: Water pressure chemically breaks down residual animal saliva in the tissue
options.B: Animal mouths harbor diverse bacteria that easily cause deep tissue infections
options.C: It permanently seals open blood vessels to stop bleeding immediately
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any tetanus prophylaxis

explanation: Animal and human mouths carry lots of germs. Flushing deep bite wounds thoroughly helps wash away bacteria before they cause ugly infections. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h5)

question: What is the go-to emergency medication for a patient in acute anaphylactic shock?
explanation: Epinephrine is a lifesaver in anaphylaxis! It quickly tightens blood vessels, opens up tight airways, and keeps the heart pumping. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h6)

question: A patient treated for a wasp sting allergy feels fine after 30 minutes and wants to go home. What should you tell them?

options.A: Explain that the patient must stay longer because a secondary reaction can happen hours later
options.B: Tell the patient that once symptoms stop, they will never have another reaction
options.C: Administer a second dose of epinephrine just to be completely safe before leaving
options.D: Discharge the patient immediately with a prescription for oral antihistamines

explanation: Allergic reactions can strike twice! We call this a biphasic reaction, meaning the patient needs to stick around for observation just in case symptoms return hours later. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h6)

question: Why are animal bite wounds often left open at first instead of being stitched up right away?

options.A: To make it easier for the patient to apply daily bandages
options.B: To prevent trapping bacteria and reducing the risk of deep infection
options.C: To let the underlying bone heal before skin closure
options.D: To allow the skin to grow back faster without scarring

explanation: If you stitch up a dirty bite right away, you trap nasty bacteria inside. Leaving it open helps prevent painful abscesses. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h7)

question: Which sign strongly suggests a patient's sting site is developing a bacterial infection days later?

options.A: Spreading erythema, warmth, and purulent discharge at the site days later
options.B: Immediate localized pain and minor itching right after the sting
options.C: Clear fluid blisters that form and heal within twenty-four hours
options.D: A small drop in blood pressure within the first five minutes

explanation: Watch out for spreading redness (erythema), feeling hot to the touch, and pus (purulent discharge)—these are classic signs that bacteria have set in. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h7)

question: What is a crucial teaching point for someone prescribed an epinephrine auto-injector for severe allergies?

options.A: Keep the device stored inside a kitchen refrigerator at all times
options.B: Demonstrate how to self-administer the device into the outer thigh and call emergency services
options.C: Use the auto-injector only after taking oral antihistamines first
options.D: Replace the device once every ten years regardless of expiration date

explanation: Make sure your patient knows how to jab that auto-injector firmly into their outer thigh, and remind them to always call for emergency help right after! [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h8)

question: Why is teaching patients how to avoid environmental hazards so important after an insect sting recovery?

options.A: It guarantees that insect populations will decrease around the home
options.B: It eliminates the patient's biological sensitivity to insect venom
options.C: It minimizes the chance of future exposure and repeat anaphylactic events
options.D: It replaces the need to carry emergency rescue medications

explanation: Prevention is key! Simple steps like wearing protective clothes keep patients out of harm's way so they don't experience another scary reaction. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T6#GNS112_U7_T6_h8)
